strengths: FreqKV presents a simple and potentially useful idea: iteratively compressing KV states with a DCT-based low-frequency representation, without adding learned compression modules or changing the base architecture.
The paper motivates the method with layer- and head-level power-spectrum measurements and clearly describes the iterative cache update, attention-sink preservation, and treatment of RoPE.

The evaluation spans language modeling, LongBench, needle retrieval, two LLM families, multiple context lengths, and retaining-ratio and RoPE ablations. The needle comparison against identically trained token dropping provides useful evidence that compressed historical information can remain accessible.
The reported bounded-cache computation, latency, and FLOP measurements suggest meaningful efficiency improvements at long sequence lengths, with small compression overhead.
weaknesses: The central downstream comparison is not controlled fairly. FreqKV models receive LongAlpaca fine-tuning, whereas several LongBench baselines are inference-time methods applied to the original model. There is no full-cache model, sliding-window model, or strong learned compression baseline trained with the same data and optimization. Consequently, LongBench gains cannot be attributed specifically to frequency-domain compression.

The language-modeling comparisons are also difficult to interpret because most Full-FT and LongLoRA numbers are imported from prior work, while FreqKV is trained in the authors' setup. Training data quantities, token budgets, and other potentially consequential conditions are not demonstrated to match. A directly trained full-cache control is essential.

The ablations do not isolate why the method works. Apart from needle retrieval, there are no comprehensive comparisons against equally sized recent-token retention, uniform subsampling, average pooling, random frequency selection, or other parameter-free transforms on perplexity and LongBench. Thus, the specific value of retaining low DCT frequencies remains under-supported.

Low spectral energy is treated as equivalent to low task-relevant information, but this implication is neither theoretically justified nor tested through frequency-band interventions. The unusual operation of applying an inverse transform of length L after a length-N DCT also deserves a clearer derivation and comparison with conventional low-pass reconstruction/downsampling.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete: peak KV/total memory, prefill latency, decoding throughput, batch-size scaling, and comparisons to optimized sparse or windowed attention implementations are absent. Timing configuration is insufficiently detailed, and the headline context-extension claims conflate bounded cache computation with actual preservation of long-range capability.

Results lack uncertainty across training seeds and statistical testing. Reproducibility is further limited by the absence of released code or sufficiently complete specifications for data sampling, evaluation preprocessing, optimizer settings, and timing methodology.

The method repeatedly remaps compressed states to cache-local positional indices, but the semantic and ordering consequences of this remapping are not analyzed. Evaluation beyond 16K is dominated by perplexity and synthetic needle retrieval, leaving robust long-range reasoning at substantially extended lengths unverified.

strengths: FreqKV is a simple, parameter-free approach: iterative low-frequency DCT truncation keeps the KV cache bounded without adding learned compression modules.
The paper evaluates two LLM families and covers language modeling, LongBench, synthetic retrieval, latency, and FLOPs.
The retaining-ratio, pre/post-RoPE, and token-dropping studies provide some useful evidence about design choices.
The reported perplexity and Needle-in-a-Haystack results suggest that frequency-domain compression may preserve useful information better than naive eviction.
weaknesses: The central downstream comparison is seriously confounded: FreqKV receives long-context supervised fine-tuning, whereas several KV-compression baselines appear to be applied to the original model without equivalent training. Improvements therefore cannot be attributed to the proposed compression method.

The empirical controls are insufficient. There is no broadly evaluated, identically trained dropping/sliding-window baseline, no simple pooling or other transform baseline, and no matched full-cache fine-tuning control for the downstream experiments.

The frequency-domain motivation is weakly established. Raw power-spectrum plots on one model and one corpus do not quantify cumulative retained energy, and high energy does not imply task relevance. Early layers do not even exhibit the asserted low-frequency concentration.
LongBench results are mixed, with meaningful regressions on several tasks. The paper reports per-task wins as “SOTA” without aggregate scores, uncertainty estimates, or repeated runs.

The Needle-in-a-Haystack experiment omits important full-cache and equivalently fine-tuned baselines. Perplexity with long histories also does not establish effective use of distant information, so the evidence for genuine context extension remains limited.

Efficiency evaluation lacks peak-memory measurements, throughput, detailed timing conditions, and comparisons against competitive methods under identical cache budgets. Reported negligible compression overhead alone does not establish end-to-end superiority.

Important implementation details are underspecified, including exact position-index handling across repeated compression, DCT/IDCT normalization and dimension changes, LoRA target modules, evaluation truncation, decoding settings, and random seeds. No code or trained artifacts are identified.
Overall, the idea is interesting but the evaluation does not isolate its contribution well enough to support the paper’s strong effectiveness and state-of-the-art claims at a top-tier venue.

strengths: FreqKV is a simple and technically interesting approach: iterative low-frequency DCT compression bounds the KV cache without adding learned compression modules or modifying the base architecture.
The motivating observation—that later-layer key and value states concentrate energy in low-frequency components—is clearly illustrated and connected coherently to the proposed method.
The evaluation covers two model families, language modeling on PG-19 and Proof-pile, LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval, context lengths up to 64K, and both latency and FLOP measurements.

Results are encouraging: FreqKV preserves strong perplexity under substantial context extension, clearly improves over simple token dropping on needle retrieval, and exhibits nearly linear total processing cost with very small measured compression overhead.
The method handles causal processing, iterative compression, attention sinks, and RoPE explicitly, making the core algorithm reasonably clear and practically relevant.
weaknesses: The LongBench comparison is not fully controlled. FreqKV receives LongAlpaca supervised fine-tuning, whereas several competing KV-compression methods appear to be applied to the original chat model. Consequently, the claimed state-of-the-art gains cannot be attributed solely to frequency-domain compression; all methods should be evaluated on identically fine-tuned backbones.

The ablations do not adequately isolate the value of low-frequency DCT compression. Comparisons with average pooling, interpolation, token merging, random or magnitude-based frequency selection, and a time-domain compression method under the same training protocol are missing. The dropping baseline alone is insufficient.

The argument that high spectral energy implies information important for attention is heuristic. No quantitative retained-energy statistics, layer-dependent analysis tied to downstream performance, or explanation of why a single compression ratio across layers and heads is appropriate is provided.

Efficiency reporting omits direct peak-memory measurements, throughput under realistic prefill-plus-generation workloads, and comparisons against efficient compressed-cache baselines. Thus, the practical advantage over methods other than full-cache attention is not established convincingly.

Reproducibility is limited: there is no code release indicated, and important details such as optimizer configuration, sequence sampling, hardware allocation, generation/evaluation settings, random seeds, and quality-result variance are absent. The quality experiments also rely mostly on single reported runs.

strengths: The core idea—iteratively low-pass filtering and resampling pre-RoPE KV states—is simple, intuitive, and potentially useful for bounded-memory long-context inference.
The paper evaluates both prefilling and decoding across language modeling, retrieval, understanding, and generation tasks, using multiple LLaMA model families and context lengths.
The reported efficiency is promising: cache size remains bounded, attention cost grows approximately linearly with total sequence length, and measured DCT overhead is very small.
Ablations examine retained frequency bands, compression ratio, sink-token count, rescaling, and compression versus recent-token dropping.
weaknesses: The central 256K context-extension claim is not convincingly established. At 64K–256K, the only quality evidence is perplexity, which is dominated by local next-token information and does not demonstrate retrieval or use of distant context. Retrieval and reasoning evaluations stop at 16K, where RULER performance is only 47.3 and the needle results visibly degrade beyond the native window.

The comparison protocol is insufficiently specified and appears potentially confounded by fine-tuning. FreqKV is trained on RedPajama or LongAlpaca, while most KV-compression baselines are described as inference-time methods; the paper does not clearly state whether every method uses the identical fine-tuned checkpoint, data, and training budget. Improvements over the full-cache model, including under 1% retention, make this ambiguity especially consequential.

The out-of-window evaluation mainly compares against cache-eviction methods that were not designed to extend positional encodings and predictably collapse past the native context limit. Relevant context-extension and recurrent-memory alternatives such as RoPE-scaled full attention, LongLoRA, Activation Beacon, InfLLM/LM-Infinite, or comparable bounded-memory approaches are absent from the key understanding and retrieval comparisons.

Energy concentration is not sufficient evidence that low-frequency components preserve task-relevant information. The synonym perturbation study can be affected by tokenization and sequence-alignment changes, and the paper lacks matched comparisons against simple pooling, interpolation, random projection, or stronger learned and non-learned resampling alternatives.

Several broad claims are overstated: iterative compression does not preserve all token information, the method requires substantial adaptation training for its main results, and changing pre-RoPE caching and position assignment is an architectural/inference-pipeline modification despite claims of being architecture-agnostic and requiring no modification.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: the abstract's code URL is blank, there is no algorithmic pseudocode or sufficiently detailed baseline protocol, and results have no uncertainty estimates or repeated-run analysis. Overall, the method is promising, but the evidence does not yet support the strongest extrapolation and superiority claims at a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper presents a simple and potentially useful idea: applying DCT-based low-pass compression to KV states and iteratively recompressing older context while preserving recent and sink tokens.

The method is described clearly, including its interaction with RoPE, rescaling, and chunk-wise processing. The empirical study covers language modeling, retrieval, understanding, and generation, with several ablations and measurements of training cost, FLOPs, and compression overhead.
Results suggest that the approach can outperform token-eviction methods under aggressive cache budgets and that compression itself adds little computational overhead.
weaknesses: The main comparisons are substantially confounded by training. FreqKV is fine-tuned to operate under compression, whereas many competing KV methods are inference-time methods applied without comparable adaptation. At 16K, several baselines collapse specifically because they use out-of-range RoPE positions, while FreqKV changes the positional treatment and is trained for extension. Thus, these experiments do not isolate the benefit of frequency-domain compression.

The strongest extrapolation claim is not convincingly validated. Stable perplexity up to 256K, measured with a sliding window of 256, does not demonstrate effective use of information from 256K tokens: next-token prediction can remain stable using only recent context. A truncated/sliding-cache baseline and long-range retrieval or reasoning evaluations at 64K–256K are necessary.

The claim that FreqKV preserves information from all tokens is inaccurate: removing high-frequency coefficients is explicitly lossy. Low spectral energy does not imply low task-relevant information, particularly for names, numbers, code, or mathematical symbols; the reported Proof-pile degradation supports this concern.

The proposed interpretation that low frequencies encode global semantics is weakly supported. The evidence is limited to averaged spectra on one model and dataset, a small synonym-perturbation experiment, and summarization results after retaining frequency halves. These observations do not establish the claimed semantic decomposition or explain why repeated recompression remains reliable.

The frequency operation is entangled with positional reindexing. Compressed pseudo-tokens are repeatedly assigned positions within the cache, changing their effective positional relationships. There is neither a theoretical analysis nor an adequate ablation separating the effects of DCT compression, position remapping, fine-tuning, and bounded-window attention.

The Dropping ablation is limited to Needle-in-a-Haystack at up to 8K. A fair learned non-frequency baseline trained under the same data, objective, cache size, and positional scheme is missing from the main benchmark suite.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete: compression-kernel overhead and FLOPs are reported, but there is no comprehensive comparison of end-to-end prefill latency, decoding throughput, and peak inference memory against strong efficient-attention or trained-compression baselines.

Results lack variance, confidence intervals, or significance analysis and are limited to relatively small LLaMA-2/3 models. The claims of architecture agnosticism, arbitrary-length processing, and robust context extension are therefore stronger than the presented evidence.

strengths: FreqKV offers a simple and potentially useful idea: compressing pre-RoPE KV states through low-frequency DCT components and applying the operation iteratively to maintain a bounded cache.

The method introduces no additional model modules and supports both prefilling and autoregressive decoding. Its treatment of sink tokens, RoPE, rescaling, and repeated compression is clearly described.
The empirical study is broad, covering two LLaMA generations, language modeling, retrieval, understanding, and long-generation benchmarks, with several recent KV-compression baselines.
The paper includes useful ablations on frequency selection, retention ratio, sink size, rescaling, and a token-dropping alternative.
The efficiency results are promising: measured compression overhead is below 0.5%, while training time, memory, and long-sequence decoding costs improve substantially.
Results at severe compression ratios are particularly interesting, and the stable PG-19 perplexity through 256K tokens motivates further study.
weaknesses: The most serious issue is a likely training confound in the downstream comparisons. FreqKV models are fine-tuned on LongAlpaca with compression, whereas the manuscript does not establish that eviction and merging baselines receive equivalent fine-tuning. Improvements on LongBench, RULER, and LongGenBench therefore cannot be cleanly attributed to the compression method rather than additional adaptation. Comparisons using identical model checkpoints and training budgets are necessary.

The headline 256K context-extension result is supported only by sliding-window perplexity. Stable perplexity does not demonstrate that information from distant parts of a 256K context remains accessible; retrieval and reasoning experiments extend only to 16K, where RULER performance is 47.3 and Needle-in-a-Haystack already shows substantial failures.

There is no direct comparison against a full-cache version of the same fine-tuned model. Consequently, the quality loss caused specifically by frequency compression, as distinct from the benefits of fine-tuning, remains unclear.

The interpretation that low frequencies encode global semantics while high frequencies encode local details is stronger than the evidence. Power concentration and robustness to synonym replacement do not uniquely establish this semantic decomposition, and cumulative retained-energy statistics across models, layers, heads, and domains are absent.

Efficiency reporting is incomplete for deployment claims: inference peak memory, end-to-end prefill latency or throughput, generation throughput, and comparisons at matched cache budgets and hardware are not comprehensively reported.

The claim that FreqKV preserves information from all tokens is imprecise because high-frequency components are explicitly discarded and repeated compression can progressively erase older details. The paper should characterize age-dependent information loss and avoid suggesting lossless preservation.

The evaluation is restricted to 7B–13B LLaMA-family models, and the weaker Proof-pile results indicate an important limitation for symbol- and detail-sensitive contexts that deserves deeper investigation.
